sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
In recent years, as environmental issues such as global warming become increasingly 
severe, the distributed generation (DG) of distributed renewable energy sources has rap-
idly developed [1–3]. The distribution network, as the main carrier of the DG, has seen a 
continuous increase in the penetration rate of the DG within it [4]. This has highlighted 
the issue of bidirectional power ﬂow [5] in distribution netw orks, which can, in severe 
cases, lead to over-voltage problems [6]. When confronted with signiﬁcant reverse power 
ﬂows, traditional regulatory equipment like  on-load tap changer (OLTC) and capacitor 
bank (CB) exhibit slow regulation speeds, an inability to output continuously, and limited 
operational ranges [7–12]. Consequently, the distribution network’s capacity to handle 
reverse power ﬂow is insuﬃcient, leading to voltage limit violations, wind and solar cur-
tailments, and other issues that hinder the further development of the distribution net-
work. 
In addressing the aforementioned challenges, ﬂexible distribution devices, exempli-
ﬁed by soft open point (SOP) [13], have garnered signi ﬁcant a tte n t i o n  i n  r e c e n t  y e a r s .  
SOPs, composed of fully controllable power electronic devices, are free from the operation 
frequency limitations of traditional mechanical switches. They allow rapid and precise 
control [14,15] of active and reactive power on connected feeders, making them an

excellent choice for addressing supply–dema nd imbalances in distribution networks, 
thereby greatly enhancing network operational e ﬃciency [16–18]. Considerable research 
has already been conducted on SOP in distribution network optimization. For instance, 
the literature [19,20] explores the working principle of SOPs in network optimization and 
establishes an optimal scheduling model by c oordinating various controllable resources, 
thus achieving optimal power ﬂow distribution. The literature [21] proposes a time-seg-
mented reactive compensation strategy. By joint optimization of an SOP and energy stor-
age systems, targeting minimization of average voltage deviation and network loss, oper-
ational eﬃciency is enhanced. The literature [22] develops a two-stage day-ahead and in-
tra-day optimization model incorporating an SOP and other ﬂexible resources, with dis-
tributed generation (DG) penetration as the objective function, improving economic e ﬃ-
ciency while boosting DG accommodation. The literature [23] establishes an active–reac-
tive coordination optimization model for the network, resolving voltage limit issues by 
regulating reactive compensation devices, photovoltaic inverters, SOPs, and other adjust-
able equipment. Additionally, several studies, including [24], address voltage issues aris-
ing from two-way power ﬂow due to increased DG penetration by establishing a bidirec-
tional transformer model to quantify control curves under bidirectional ﬂow and mitigat-
ing voltage ﬂuctuations through multi-layer regulation of energy storage devices. How-
ever, there is limited research on detailed modeling of reverse power ﬂow transmission 
capacity in distribution networks and on utilizing SOP ﬂexibility to address challenges of 
insuﬃcient reverse power ﬂow transmission capability. 
Based on the aforementioned issues, this paper’s contributions are as follows: 
(1) It analyzes the impact of OLTC parameters, the OLTC’s low-voltage side reactive 
compensation, and DG installation location  on the reverse power flow capacity of 
distribution networks. A refined model is established, enabling precise calculations 
of reverse power flow capacity considering these influencing factors. 
(2) Addressing the issue of insufficient reve rse power flow capacity in distribution 
networks, a multi-distribution network joint operation optimization model is 
established based on an SOP. This interconnects multiple distribution networks via 
an SOP, enhancing the reverse power flow capacity of individual networks, thus 
improving the overall operational efficiency of the distribution network. 
(3) Using the improved IEEE 33-node system, the paper examines the optimization role 
of an SOP when introduced in various op erational scenarios, impacting the reverse 
power flow capacity and overall operational efficiency of the distribution network. 
2. Analysis of Factors Aﬀecting Reverse Power Flow Transmission Capacity in  
Distribution Networks 
Reverse power ﬂow in a distribution network occu rs when the output from the DG 
exceeds the load demand of the distribution network, causing power to ﬂow backward to 
the upstream grid. The reverse power ﬂow capacity in distribution networks is inﬂuenced 
by the following three factors: The ﬁrst factor is the paramete rs of the OL TC connected 
between the distribution network and the upstream grid, including the rated capacity of 
the OLTC, the di ﬀerence in the per unit values of voltage on both sides of the OLTC, as 
well as the allowable maximum and minimum tap changer ratios. The second factor is the 
capacity of reactive power compensation that can be deployed on the low-voltage side of 
the OLTC. The third factor is the electrical di stance from the DG to the low-voltage side 
of the OLTC. 
First, the nameplate-rated capacity of the OLTC directly determines the maximum 
reverse power ﬂow that can be transmitted. Additionally, the magnitude of reverse power 
ﬂow during transmission is proportional to the diﬀerence in the per unit values of voltage 
on both sides of the OLTC. Therefore, the greater the di ﬀerence, the larger the reverse 
power ﬂow capacity. Since the per unit value of the high-voltage side remains constant 
and is lower than that of the low-voltage side during operation, with increasing 
Appl. Sci. 2024, 14, 11797 3 of 27 
 
transmission capacity, the per unit value of  the low-voltage side voltage increases. Con-
sequently, the OLTC’s transformation ratio also increases. When this ratio reaches its up-
per limit, further increase in reverse power ﬂow capacity is not possible. 
Regarding the reactive power compensation capacity on the low-voltage side of the 
OLTC, to maintain the power factor of the OLTC primary side (low-voltage side during 
reverse ﬂow) at the required value, as the reverse power ﬂow capacity increases, more 
reactive compensation capacity is required on the low-voltage side. Once the full compen-
sation capacity is utilized, further increase in reverse power ﬂow capacity is not possible. 
Concerning the electrical distance from th e DG to the OLTC’s low-voltage side, as 
the reverse power ﬂow capacity increases, the voltage drop along the line from the DG to 
OLTC also increases [25]. When this voltage drop reaches its allowable maximum, further 
increase in transmission capacity necessaril y requires reduced allowable electrical dis-
tance between the DG and the OLTC to prevent voltage limit violations [26,27]. When the 
electrical distance is reduced to zero, me aning the DG node coincides with the OLTC’s 
low-voltage side node, any further capacity increase is not possible.

sections.title: 2.2 Reactive Power Compensation on the Low-Voltage Side of Oil-Immersed Tap Changers
sections.text:
Inﬂuences Reverse Power Flow Capacity 
During OLTC operation, reactive power compensation must be applied on both sides 
to maintain power factor. In the presence of forward power ﬂow, the power factor of the 
upstream grid might not meet the OLTC’s primary requirements. Hence, reactive power 
is added on the high-voltage (primary) side to adjust the power factor. Also, considering 
the mismatch between the OLTC’s low-voltage (secondary) side power factor and the dis-
tribution network’s power factor, reactive compensation is introduced on the low-voltage 

Appl. Sci. 2024, 14, 11797 6 of 27 
 
side as well. In reverse power ﬂow scenarios, due to the high-power factor derived from 
DG units, capacitive reactive power is introduced on the low-voltage (primary) side to 
lower the power factor. Similarly, as the OLT C’s internal reactive losses surpass active 
losses, capacitive reactive power is added to the high-voltage (secondary) side to maintain 
the power factor. To facilitate the analysis of changes in active and reactive power, based 
on Figure 1, this paper empl oys the tangent value of the po wer factor angle to describe 
the aforementioned compensation process. For forward power ﬂow, the tangent values of 
the power factor angle on both sides of the OLTC can be expressed as follows:

sections.title: 4 Joint Operation Optimization Model for Multi-Distribution Networks with SOP
sections.text:
Considering Reverse Power Flow 
Since the maximum value of 𝑆ଶ,௥௘,௧,௠௔௫
∗  in the distribution ne twork is only about 50% 
of the OLTC’s rated capacity, it limits furt her development. To address this issue, this 
paper employs a soft open point (SOP) to ﬂexibly interconnect multiple distribution grids. 
This enables sharing of backward power transfer capacities among sub-distribution net-
works and enhances the grid’s capacity to handle reverse ﬂow under high penetration of 
the DG. Figure 8 illustrates the SOP interco nnection schematic, where the SOP interlinks 
two distribution networks at an equivalent power source node. When the reverse power 
ﬂow in distribution network 1 exceeds its maximum transferable capacity, the SOP diverts 
the excess power to distribution network 2, which then transmits it to the upstream grid, 
thus reducing occurrences of wind and solar energy curtailment. 

Appl. Sci. 2024, 14, 11797 13 of 27 
 
 
Figure 8. The SOP interconnects two distribution networks.

sections.title: 4.1 Fundamental Principles and Mathematical Models of SOP
sections.text:
This paper employs a back-to-back voltage source converter (B2B VSC) to implement 
the SOP. The number of ports is determined by the count of AC/DC bidirectional convert-
ers, which are internally connected through a DC/DC converter. The AC side of the 
AC/DC converter links to the distribution network feeders, while the DC side connects to 
the DC/DC converter, enabling interconnection between di ﬀerent feeders. The basic to-
pology is illustrated in the Figure 9. 
 
Figure 9. The SOP’s basic topological structure. 
Under normal operating conditions, the two-end SOP selects a PQ-Vdc control mode, 
while the three-end SOP employs a PQ-PQ-Vdc Q control mode. This means that one VSC 
regulates the DC-side voltage, and the ot her VSCs control the power being transmi tted. 
The operational variables of the SOP include the active and reactive power transmitted by 
the VSCs, with speciﬁc operational constraints as follows [28,29]:
